title: Hearts that tremble
hookLine: believers are those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned (8:2)

lines: FROM THE HANDS TO THE HEARTS.
cards: Surah eight is al-Anfal, the Spoils, revealed in Medina after the battle of Badr, in the second year after the emigration: the first major clash between the young Muslim community and the Quraysh of Mecca.
It opens on an awkward note. Right after the battle, the companions are arguing over the spoils, who gets what, who earned more.
The first verse says the spoils belong to Allah and the messenger, so be mindful, and set things right between you. Then the second verse turns from what's in their hands to what's in their hearts.

teach.b: In Pickthall's words: “They only are the (true) believers whose hearts feel fear when Allah is mentioned.” The verb is wajilat: their hearts tremble, quake, shiver with awe.
Pickthall says fear, and the early commentators kept that sense: al-Suddi pictured a man about to do wrong who is told, fear God, and his heart trembles, and he stops.
But the word holds awe as well, the shiver at the edge of something enormous. The verse goes on: when His verses are recited to them, their faith increases, and they put their trust in their Lord.
Then verse three: they establish the prayer and spend from what We've given them.
Notice the order: a heart that moves, faith that grows, trust, then prayer and giving. The outward follows the inward.

And faith can increase; many scholars took this verse as evidence that faith isn't a fixed amount, but rises and falls. Here's a puzzle, though. Surah thirteen says that in the remembrance of Allah, hearts find rest.
So which is it, trembling or rest? Commentators answered: both.
Surah thirty-nine says it in one breath: skins shiver at the recitation, then skins and hearts soften toward the remembrance of Allah. First the shiver, then the softening.

A heart that never trembles at anything might be calm, or simply numb. Coming right after a quarrel over spoils, these verses seem to say: if the heart is moved by the right thing, the hands will stop grabbing.

how: Muslims read 8:2–4 as a portrait of the believer; many scholars cite 8:2 to teach that faith increases and decreases, and recitation is valued for moving the heart.

games.why: it moves from the hands to the hearts: true believers are those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned.

practice: Think back over the last month to a time your heart actually moved: a piece of music, a child's laugh, a verse, a funeral, a sunrise, a stranger's kindness.
Remember it in detail until you feel even a faint echo of it now, notice where that feeling lives in your body, and rest there.
